subject: Business Models
title: The East India Companies
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The East India Companies.

hook.text: In 1602, the Dutch East India Company became the world's first publicly traded corporation.

buildup.text: It issued stock, paid dividends, and had a board of directors—a structure still used by every public company.

discovery.text: At its peak, it was worth $7.9 trillion in today's dollars—larger than Apple and Google combined.

twist.text: It also had a private army and the power to wage war. Corporation and empire were one.

climax.text: The East India model proved that shared ownership could fund ventures beyond any individual's wealth.

punchline.text: The first IPO funded spice ships, not tech startups.

quiz.question: What made the Dutch East India Company historically significant?

details.summary: The British and Dutch East India Companies were the world's first multinational corporations, granted government monopolies on Asian trade. The Dutch VOC became the first publicly traded company, issuing shares on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange..
details.whyItMatters: East India Companies invented the corporate structures that power modern business: joint-stock ownership, public share trading, limited liability, and professional management..
takeaways: The Dutch VOC was the first publicly traded company on the first stock exchange
These companies had private armies and governed entire territories for profit
They invented joint-stock ownership and limited liability for shareholders

faq.question: Why were East India Companies structured as joint-stock corporations?
faq.answer: Asian trade voyages required enormous capital with high risk of loss from storms, piracy, and war. Joint-stock structure let many investors pool capital while limiting each one's liability to their investment..

faq.question: How powerful were the East India Companies compared to modern corporations?
faq.answer: The Dutch VOC at its peak had a market value equivalent to over 7 trillion modern dollars, employed over 50,000 people, had a private army of 10,000 soldiers, and governed entire regions of Southeast Asia. No modern corporation approaches this level of sovereign power.
